<strong>Componer.</strong> La B entra en: Composing. B enters $\rho$ and comes out as F; F enters $\sigma$ and comes out as the next one, which on passing the last wraps round to the beginning: A. So $\sigma\rho(B) = A$.
<strong>Conjugar.</strong> Si se renombr: Conjugating. If the letters are renamed by swapping A and B, the cycle (AC) becomes (BC) and (BFDE) becomes (AFDE): the lengths are still $2 + 4$. That is what Rejewski exploited.
<strong>El orden importa.</strong> Al re: Order matters. The other way round, $\rho\sigma(B)$: B shifts to C, and $\rho(C) = A$. Here they agree, but with D they do not: $\sigma\rho(D) = \sigma(E) = F$ and $\rho\sigma(D) = \rho(E) = B$. Permutations do not commute, and that is why Enigma's formula has an order.
<strong>Los ciclos de $\\rho$.</strong>: The cycles of $\rho$. A→C→A: a cycle of length 2. B→F→D→E→B: a cycle of length 4. Structure: $2 + 4$.
Al revés: con Enigma la probabilidad de: The other way round: with Enigma the probability that they match is zero. That none matches is exactly what is expected of a correct hypothesis.
Antes de la bomba hubo una idea aún más: Before the bombe there was an even more elegant idea. In the nineteen-thirties, each message began with the message key enciphered twice: six letters. Marian Rejewski realised that letter 1 and letter 4 were the same original letter enciphered at two different positions, so by composing the two permutations a known permutation was obtained, and after a few of the day's messages, the whole of it. And that permutation had a property that did not depend on the plugboard: the lengths of its cycles.
Arthur Scherbius patentó Enigma en 1918: Arthur Scherbius patented Enigma in 1918 and sold it to banks and armies. Marian Rejewski, a 27-year-old mathematician of the Polish Cipher Bureau, reconstructed the rotors' wiring at the end of 1932 with group theory and some documents bought from a spy, and with Jerzy Różycki and Henryk Zygalski read the German traffic for years. In July 1939, weeks before the invasion, they handed everything over to the French and the British. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman designed the bombe in 1940, and the breaking of Enigma, called Ultra, shortened the war by two years or more according to historians.
Cada rotor es un disco con 26 contactos: Each rotor is a disc with 26 contacts on each side, joined by wires in a fixed order: a permutation $\rho$ of the 26 letters. If the rotor did not turn, the machine would be a fixed substitution. But it turns: at position $i$, the signal enters $i$ contacts higher up and leaves $i$ lower down. El reflector $U$ une los contactos de do: The reflector $U$ joins the contacts in pairs: A with Y, B with R… It is a permutation that is its own inverse, with no fixed point. And since the signal comes back through the same rotors in reverse, the whole machine satisfies $E^{-1} = E$: if A enciphers as Q, then Q enciphers as A, with the same settings. That was extremely convenient: deciphering was typing the ciphertext. But it had a mathematical consequence the designers overlooked: no letter can be enciphered as itself. If $E(x) = x$, the current would have to cross the reflector and come back along the same path, and the reflector joins no contact to itself.
El reflector hace $E = E^{-1}$: descifra: The reflector makes $E = E^{-1}$: deciphering is typing the ciphertext. In exchange, no letter enciphers as itself, and that aligns the cribs.

Enigma era una máquina de escribir con b: Enigma was a typewriter with light bulbs. A letter was pressed, a current crossed a plugboard, three wired rotors, a reflector, the three rotors again and the plugboard, and the bulb of the enciphered letter lit up. After each letter, a rotor turned one position. It was, in effect, a Vigenère with a different alphabet for each letter and a period of $26^3 = 17\,576$: frequency analysis had nothing to count.
Enigma se rompió con matemáticas y cribs: Enigma was broken with mathematics and cribs, not with brute force: $10^{23}$ keys were of no use at all.
Esa restricción fue la palanca de los cr: That restriction was the lever of the cribs: the Germans sent weather reports and fixed formulas, and a probable text placed under the ciphertext, with no letter-by-letter match, gave a handful of equations about the machine's settings. Turing and Welchman's bombe was a device that tested the 17,576 rotor positions against those equations in about twenty minutes.

The second formula is the whole machine: the plugboard $P$, the three rotors, the reflector $U$, and back through the same rotors in reverse and through the plugboard. It reads from right to left, because the signal enters through $P$. Each letter pressed changes the $i$, so $E$ changes with every letter.

It reads: “if tau is the conjugate of pi by P, then tau and pi have the same cycle structure”. Conjugating by $P$ is only changing the names of the letters: a cycle of length 5 is still a cycle of length 5 with other letters.

The plugboard, with its hundreds of billions of possibilities, was a conjugation. Rejewski swept it aside at a stroke: the cycle lengths depended only on the order and position of the rotors, $6\cdot 17\,576 = 105\,456$ cases. He catalogued them all with a machine, the cyclometer, and the catalogue returned the day's key in minutes.
